title: Nonhelema
summary: Nonhelema, sister of Shawnee leader Cornstalk, was a Chalakatha chief, diplomat, and warrior who held influence at Lower Shawneetown on the Ohio River.
bodyMarkdown:
Settlers who met Nonhelema remembered how tall she was. She stood nearly six and a half feet, and they nicknamed her "the Grenadier," after the tall soldiers of the day. Among her own people, the [Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee), she mattered for other reasons. She was a chief, a warrior and a diplomat.

She spent much of her life trying to keep her people out of other nations' wars.

Nonhelema Hokolesqua was born around 1718 into the Chalakatha (Chillicothe) division of the Shawnee and spent her early years in Pennsylvania. She was the sister of [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader)), who later became one of the best-known Shawnee leaders of his time. By about 1750 she was a chief with real influence at [Lower Shawneetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Shawneetown), the Shawnee town on the Ohio River in what is now Greenup County, Kentucky.

She knew war firsthand. During [Pontiac's War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pontiac%27s_War), she was at the [Battle of Bushy Run](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Bushy_Run) in 1763. When the American Revolution reached the Ohio country, she and Cornstalk argued that the Shawnee should stay neutral. In the summer of 1777, she warned the Americans that some Shawnee had gone to Detroit to join the British.

That fall, American militiamen murdered Cornstalk while he was held at [Fort Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Randolph_(West_Virginia)). Even so, Nonhelema kept helping the Americans. She warned Fort Randolph and Fort Donnally of coming attacks, and she disguised two messengers in Native clothing so they could carry a warning to Fort Donnally. Her cattle were destroyed in revenge, and she led her followers to the Coshocton area, near the Lenape leader White Eyes.

In 1780 she worked as a guide and interpreter for Augustin de La Balme's expedition toward the Illinois country.

In 1785 she asked Congress for 1,000 acres in Ohio in return for her service. Congress gave her a pension instead: daily rations, plus blankets and clothing each year. The next year, Kentucky militia under Benjamin Logan [attacked the Shawnee towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan%27s_raid) where she lived. Her husband, the chief [Moluntha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moluntha), was killed after he was taken prisoner.

Nonhelema was captured and held at Fort Pitt. While she was held there, she helped put together a list of Shawnee words. She was later released, and she died in December 1786.

## Kentucky today

Lower Shawneetown is remembered in Greenup County as one of the major Shawnee towns of the Ohio Valley in the 1700s. Nonhelema's life reminds us that Shawnee leaders made hard choices about war and peace. Even her loyalty to the United States did not protect her people's homes.
